name: Redpill / bluepill / purplepill frameworks

lead: The pill frameworks borrow the red/blue pill choice from The Matrix to label worldviews about gender, dating and social status. Red pill is adopted from manosphere circles, blue pill is its opposite, and black pill is a more fatalistic version from incel forums.
Purple pill is used inconsistently across communities.

paras: They work as shorthand identities: members describe having 'woken up' to a supposed hidden truth about social hierarchies.
Researchers and advocacy groups have criticized some of these frameworks, particularly the black pill, as fatalistic or extremist.

web.title: Red pill and blue pill - Wikipedia

lead: The 'pill' frameworks are color-coded metaphors, borrowed from the 1999 film The Matrix, that online communities use to describe worldviews about dating, gender and social status. In the film, a red pill lets the character Neo see reality and a blue pill returns him to blissful ignorance.[1]

The terms were adopted by the antifeminist 'manosphere'; Wikipedia reports the subreddit r/TheRedPill was started in 2012 and was quarantined by Reddit in September 2018.[1] The 'black pill' emerged on incel forums as a more nihilistic variant, and adherents of related frameworks such as the 'purple pill' use their own definitions. Scholars and advocacy groups have analyzed these frameworks critically.[1][2]

paras: Wikipedia traces the red-pill trope to the 1990 film Total Recall and, in its best-known form, to The Matrix, where Morpheus offers Neo the choice.[1] Curtis Yarvin popularized the metaphor in right-wing politics in a 2007 essay, according to the same article.[1]

Within the manosphere, 'taking the red pill' means accepting its ideology, while those who reject it are called 'blue pilled'; core beliefs cited include hypergamy and 'AWALT' (all women are like that).[1]

The black pill, described on incel forums, adds fatalism: it holds that escaping a low rung of a social hierarchy is impossible.[1][2] Sources in the set do not give a settled definition of the purple pill, which is used differently across communities.

Researchers such as Debbie Ging and Shawn Van Valkenburgh analyze the manosphere's ideology critically, according to Wikipedia.[1] Organizations including the Anti-Defamation League and the Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism have described parts of the incel black pill as extremist or death-cult-like.[2]
No studies found on the color-pill frameworks as a whole. Research on the black pill within incel communities is covered in the Blackpill article.

timeline.event: The Matrix is released, popularizing the red/blue pill choice.[1]
Curtis Yarvin's essay uses red pills as a political metaphor.[1]
